Analyzing the Conflict Between Industrial Growth (SDG 9) and Climate Action (SDG13)

Dorothy Worbie

Executive Summary

  1. The analysis initially flagged a misleading policy paradox: that Innovation (SDG 9) created an unavoidable trade-off with Climate Action (SDG 13).The deeper analysis resolved this paradox, showing the negative link disappears when controlling for Unsustainable Consumption (SDG 12) and Sustainable Cities (SDG 11).The conflict isn’t with innovation itself, but with how that innovation is consumed and deployed. The true policy challenge is not limiting SDG 9, but rather directing it by addressing SDG 12 and SDG 11.

1. Data Preparation and Initial Exploration

1.1 Data Source and Initial Preparation

This dataset, originally sourced as a **.xlsx file from the Sustainable Development Report website, underwent initial cleaning and preparation in Microsoft Excel. This involved removing duplicate entries, ensuring consistent data formatting and correcting typographical errors. Additionally, minor descriptive statistical analysis was performed in Excel to gain a foundational understanding of the data structure. The current file imported into R is a pre-processed version, and all other subsequent in-depth statistical analysis, modelling and visualizations will be done using R.

1.2 Installing packages and loading libraries

1.3 Importing & Cleaning

# Reading the dataset
Correlation.Data <- read.csv("/Users/D./Downloads/Correlation Data.csv", header = TRUE) 

sdg_data <- read.csv("/Users/D./Downloads/Correlation Data.csv", header = TRUE) 

sdg_data <- Correlation.Data 

# Inspecting the first few rows and structure to confirm successful import

# View(sdg_data)  # Commented out for smooth  knitting

str(sdg_data)

##  $ Country: chr  "Afghanistan" "Angola" "Albania" "Andorra" ...
##  $ goal9  : int  14 20 43 62 83 50 53 61 90 98 ...
##  $ goal13 : int  99 94 88 87 10 90 91 83 28 71 ...
head(sdg_data)
##                Country goal9 goal13

# Data import and removing NA values

sdg_analysis <- sdg_data %>% 
  
  # Remov NAs first
  na.omit() %>%

                sdg_13 = goal13) %>%

  # Force R to use the dplyr::select function
  
  dplyr::select(Country, sdg_9, sdg_13)

1.4 Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)

Visual Inspection (Histograms) - justify the choice of a non-parametric test (Spearman’s ρ).

# Distribution of SDG 9 scores (Outlier/Skewness Check)

ggplot(sdg_analysis, aes(x = sdg_9)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = "#4169E1", color = "black") +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of SDG 9 Scores", 
    x = "SDG 9 Score", 
    y = "Count of Countries"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# Box plot for SDG 13 to identify specific outliers

ggplot(sdg_analysis, aes(y = sdg_13)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#4169E1", color = "black") +
  labs(
    title = "Box Plot of SDG 13 Scores (Outlier Check)", 
    y = "SDG 13 Score"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

Observation: The skewed distribution (especially for SDG 13) proves the importance of using Spearman’s Rank Correlation as a better option for focus on ranks instead of raw numbers, for data reliability (in this case with messy data and extreme outliers).

2. Correlational Analysis and Reliability

2.1 Calculating and Testing Spearman’s ρ

# Formally testing the Spearman's rank correlation coefficient (ρ) 

spearman_test_result <- cor.test(sdg_analysis$sdg_9, 
                                  sdg_analysis$sdg_13, 
                                  method = "spearman", 
                                  exact = FALSE)

print(spearman_test_result)
## 
##  Spearman's rank correlation rho
## 
## data:  sdg_analysis$sdg_9 and sdg_analysis$sdg_13
## S = 2655359, p-value < 2.2e-16
## alternative hypothesis: true rho is not equal to 0
## sample estimates:
##        rho 
## -0.7962785

2.2 Visualizing the Rank Relationship

plot(rank(sdg_analysis$sdg_9), rank(sdg_analysis$sdg_13), 
     main = expression(paste("Spearman Rank Correlation Visualization (", rho, " = -0.796)")),
     xlab = "Rank of SDG 9 (Innovation)", 
     ylab = "Rank of SDG 13 (Climate Action)")

2.3 Data Reliability Check (Kendall’s τ)

# Confirming robustness using the alternative non-parametric coefficient, Kendall's Tau (τ)
kendall_test <- cor.test(sdg_analysis$sdg_9, 
                         sdg_analysis$sdg_13, 
                         method = "kendall")

print(kendall_test)
## 
##  Kendall's rank correlation tau
## 
## data:  sdg_analysis$sdg_9 and sdg_analysis$sdg_13
## z = -13.051, p-value < 2.2e-16
## alternative hypothesis: true tau is not equal to 0
## sample estimates:
##        tau 
## -0.6240675

3. Investigating Confounding Variables

Investigating granular drivers like SDG Goals 7, 11, etc. for further investigation.

3.1 Merging and Ordering the Full Dataset

# Loading the second dataset containing sdg_6, sdg_7, sdg_11, sdg_12 and merging to previous dataframe used for earlier analysis

new_sdg_data <- read.csv("/Users/D./Downloads/New correlation data.csv", header = TRUE) 

sdg_analysis_merged <- merge(
    x = sdg_analysis, 
    y = new_sdg_data, 
    by = "Country", 
    all.x = FALSE
)

# Checking first few rows
head(sdg_analysis_merged)
##               Country sdg_9 sdg_13 sdg_6 sdg_7 sdg_11 sdg_12
## 1         Afghanistan    14     99    51    34     34     95
## 2             Albania    43     88    83    87     90     77
## 3             Algeria    46     90    59    67     70     88
## 4             Andorra    62     87   100    77     99     30
## 5              Angola    20     94    55    46     42     94
## 6 Antigua and Barbuda    61     83    82    67     98     73
# Assigning the final, processed data frame to sdg_analysis_cleaned

sdg_analysis_cleaned <- sdg_analysis_merged %>%
  
  # 1. Cleaning the data to remove NA rows resulting from the merge
  na.omit() %>%
  
# Resetting the row names to be sequential (1, 2, 3...) to make indexing by position reliable.
  
  tibble::rowid_to_column("index") %>%
  
  # 2. Arranging the columns in  order for easy readability
  dplyr::select(
    Country,
    sdg_6, 
    sdg_7, 
    sdg_9,
    sdg_11, 
    sdg_12, 
    sdg_13
  )

# Confirming the cleaned dataframe 
head(sdg_analysis_cleaned)

3.2 Partial Correlation (Controlling for SDG 11)

The rationale is to use the SDG_11 as a proxy for infrastructural/development to verify if the conflict is simply due to wealth.

# Calculate the Spearman partial correlation (SDG 9 vs. SDG 13, controlling for SDG 11)
partial_rho_11 <- pcor.test(sdg_analysis_cleaned$sdg_9, 
                            sdg_analysis_cleaned$sdg_13, 
                            sdg_analysis_cleaned$sdg_11, 
                            method = "spearman")

print(partial_rho_11)
##     estimate      p.value statistic   n gp   Method
## 1 -0.6467123 1.137069e-25 -12.08053 206  1 spearman

3.3 Granular Correlation Matrix

Rationale is to identify which goals have the strongest relationships with the main variables (SDG 9 & SDG 13).

# Creating a Subset of the data for the six relevant goals

sdg_subset <- sdg_analysis_cleaned[, c("sdg_6", "sdg_7", "sdg_9", "sdg_11", "sdg_12", "sdg_13")]

# Calculating  the Spearman correlation matrix

cor_matrix <- cor(sdg_subset, method = "spearman", use = "complete.obs")

print(cor_matrix)
##             sdg_6      sdg_7      sdg_9     sdg_11     sdg_12     sdg_13
## sdg_6   1.0000000  0.7946536  0.7465067  0.7084638 -0.7342945 -0.6657148
## sdg_7   0.7946536  1.0000000  0.7417225  0.6584296 -0.7290929 -0.6378758
## sdg_9   0.7465067  0.7417225  1.0000000  0.6579118 -0.8474378 -0.7955778
## sdg_11  0.7084638  0.6584296  0.6579118  1.0000000 -0.7415445 -0.6411449
## sdg_12 -0.7342945 -0.7290929 -0.8474378 -0.7415445  1.0000000  0.8761055
## sdg_13 -0.6657148 -0.6378758 -0.7955778 -0.6411449  0.8761055  1.0000000
# 2. Plotting the Heatmap to show which goals exhibit the strongest positive and negative correlations.

ggcorrplot(
  cor_matrix,
  hc.order = TRUE, #  Hierarchical clustering for reordering
  type = "lower",  #  Showing  only the lower triangle
  lab = TRUE,      # Show correlation coefficient values
  tl.cex = 10,     
  title = "Spearman Correlation Heatmap of SDGs (Full Model Selection)"
)

4. Final Causal Quantification (Multiple Linear Regression)

4.1 Building the Final Model and Visualizing the Trio Relationship

The goal of the final model is to see if the negative link between SDG 9 (Innovation) and SDG 13 (Climate Action) is misleading by controlling for SDG 12 (Consumption) and SDG 11 (Cities).

# Building the model: SDG 13 explained by SDG 9, SDG 12, and SDG 11
final_model <- lm(sdg_13 ~ sdg_9 + sdg_12 + sdg_11, 
                  data = sdg_analysis_cleaned)

summary(final_model)
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = sdg_13 ~ sdg_9 + sdg_12 + sdg_11, data = sdg_analysis_cleaned)
## 
## Residuals:
##     Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
## -49.133  -2.357   1.919   5.990  40.885 
## 
## Coefficients:
##             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept) -0.90200   12.11172  -0.074 0.940707    
## sdg_9       -0.04784    0.06200  -0.772 0.441301    
## sdg_12       0.91768    0.09991   9.185  < 2e-16 ***
## sdg_11       0.22680    0.06600   3.436 0.000716 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 12.61 on 202 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.5263, Adjusted R-squared:  0.5193 
## F-statistic: 74.82 on 3 and 202 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16
# --- Visualizing the Core Causal Trio (SDG 9, 12, 13) ---
 
# Creating a Subset for the three key variables

sdg_trio <- sdg_analysis_cleaned %>% 
  dplyr::select(sdg_9, sdg_12, sdg_13)

# Calculating the Spearman correlation matrix for only the trio

trio_cor_matrix <- cor(sdg_trio, method = "spearman", use = "complete.obs")

# Plotting the correlation matrix for the three key variables 

ggcorrplot(
    trio_cor_matrix,
    hc.order = FALSE, # No hierarchical clustering needed for 3 vars
    type = "lower",  
    lab = TRUE,      
    tl.cex = 12,     
    title = "Correlation Trio: Innovation, Consumption, and Climate"
)

 # Key Conclusion: The coefficient for SDG 9 is non-significant, while SDG 12 has the strongest, highly significant positive effect on poor SDG  13 scores.

4.2 Visualizing Final Model Coefficients (Statistical Significance)

This plot visually represents the final proof that shows which variables are real problems for the climate and which ones are not.

# Extracting and calculating CIs using the built-in confint() function

model_summary <- as.data.frame(summary(final_model)$coefficients)
model_summary$Predictor <- rownames(model_summary)

# Calculating  95% Confidence Intervals

conf_intervals <- confint(final_model)
model_summary$Lower_CI <- conf_intervals[, 1]
model_summary$Upper_CI <- conf_intervals[, 2]

# Filtering out the intercept for cleaner plotting

model_data <- model_summary[-1, ]

# Creating the visualization
coef_plot <- ggplot(model_data, aes(x = Estimate, y = Predictor)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = Lower_CI, xmax = Upper_CI), 
                 height = 0.2, color = "darkred") +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "black") +
  scale_y_discrete(labels = c(
    "sdg_9" = "SDG 9 (Innovation)",
    "sdg_12" = "SDG 12 (Consumption)",
    "sdg_11" = "SDG 11 (Cities)"
  )) +
  labs(
    title = "Independent Effect of SDGs on Climate Action (SDG 13)",
    subtitle = "95% Confidence Intervals shown. Crossing the dashed line means non-significant.",
    x = "Coefficient Estimate",
    y = "Predictor Variable"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))
## Warning: `geom_errobarh()` was deprecated in ggplot2 4.0.0.
## ℹ Please use the `orientation` argument of `geom_errorbar()` instead.
## This warning is displayed once every 8 hours.
## Call `lifecycle::last_lifecycle_warnings()` to see where this warning was
## generated.
print(coef_plot)

4.3 Residual Analysis and Outlier Identification

Finding the difference between the country’s Actual SDG 13 score and its SDG 13 score predicted by the model based on its wealth proxies SDG 9,SDG 11, SDG 12.

___ Positive Residuals Policy is working better than expected and negative Residuals Policy is underperforming relative to capacity___

# 1. Calculate the residuals (Policy-Residual Gap: Actual SDG 13 - Predicted SDG 13)

sdg_analysis_cleaned$residual_gap <- residuals(final_model)

# 2. Identifying the top 5 Positive and Negative Outliers (The Decouplers and the Missed Opportunities)

outliers_df <- sdg_analysis_cleaned %>%
  dplyr::select(Country, sdg_13, residual_gap) %>%
  
  # Arrange by the residual gap (positive means better than expected)
  
  arrange(desc(residual_gap))

# Display Top 5 Champions (Positive Residuals)

cat("\n--- Top 5 Decoupling Champions (Positive Residuals) ---\n")
## 
## --- Top 5 Decoupling Champions (Positive Residuals) ---
print(head(outliers_df, 5))
##               Country sdg_13 residual_gap
## 1             Andorra     87     40.88452
## 2 St. Kitts and Nevis     88     27.66759
## 3            Barbados     89     23.51942
## 4          Seychelles     87     22.92236
## 5             Ireland     69     19.35042
# Display Top 5 Missed Opportunities (Negative Residuals)

cat("\n--- Top 5 Missed Opportunities (Negative Residuals) ---\n")
## 
## --- Top 5 Missed Opportunities (Negative Residuals) ---
print(tail(outliers_df, 5))

# 3. Identifying the  country names of the  specific indices (4, 27, 195)


target_indices <- c(4, 27, 194) 
outlier_countries_by_index <- sdg_analysis_cleaned[target_indices, ]

cat("\n--- Countries corresponding to key indices (4, 27, 194) ---\n")

print(outlier_countries_by_index %>% 
 dplyr::select(Country, sdg_13, residual_gap))
